Temple // an agent-native, governed data layer

The Temple Manual

Temple is one PostgreSQL database you own, fronted by a single MCP server that acts as a bouncer. Issue tracker, docs, and wiki are not separate products, they are verified schemas on top of the same store. Humans sign in through a thin web app; agents connect over MCP; both pass through the same rules, the same audit trail. This manual takes you from the idea to running it, authoring your own schemas, and the full tool cookbook.

What Temple is

Three sentences. Temple is a generalised platform: one org-scoped Postgres store where every entity for every app lives in one table, governed by one engine. On top of that store sit blueprints, verified specs that declare entity types, typed properties, and optionally a state machine with guards, invariants, and per-role policy. Everything that reads or writes, a human through the web app or an agent through MCP, passes through the same pipeline, so the rules live in one place and nothing mutates data without leaving an audit row.

Why own the data layer Run it in two minutes How a write is governed Every MCP tool Keep data private or shared Hands-on recipes

The thesis

Teams rent their interfaces. The tracker, the docs tool, the wiki are each a separate SaaS that owns your data, exposes a partial API, and forces every integration through whatever surface the vendor chose this quarter. Add agents and it compounds: each agent learns a different product, a different permission model, a different set of webhooks, and none of them share a source of truth. You end up with copies of state scattered across tools that disagree, and no single place where the rules live.

Temple inverts it. Stop renting interfaces, own one governed data layer. Every read and write goes through one door. The rules that matter, who can do what, which state changes are legal, which invariants must always hold, live in code and verified schemas, not scattered across vendor settings pages. Once that layer exists, the tracker, the docs, the wiki are just schemas on the same store.

The betThe durable thing is not the interface, it is the governed data and the rules around it. Interfaces are cheap and increasingly generated on demand. Governance is not.

Architecture

Two callers, one engine. The web app handles only login, roles, and settings. Everything else is agents talking to the MCP server. Both hit the same bouncer, the same policy gate, the same audit trail. There is no privileged side door around the engine.

Agent (Claude) ──tool call──▶ MCP server ─┐ │ ┌─────────────────────────┐ Web UI (login / roles) ──────────▶ HTTP app ─┼──▶ │ THE ENGINE (bouncer) │ ──▶ PostgreSQL │ │ 1 authenticate -> role │ entities │ │ 2 policy gate │ entity_transitions (audit) │ │ 3 space access │ entity_snapshots (versions) │ │ 4 guard + invariant │ revisions │ │ 5 typed effects │ blueprints (verified specs) │ │ 6 apply + audit (1 tx) │ spaces / grants (access) └─────┴─────────────────────────┘

The apply, audit, and snapshot writes run in a single transaction, so a change and its audit and version land together or not at all. The layers, by directory:

  • Engine (src/engine): schema registry, the L1 to L4 verifier, the transition pipeline, typed effects, the generic entity repo.
  • Auth (src/auth): scrypt passwords, cookie sessions (7-day TTL), the RBAC matrix, and the spaces/grants access layer.
  • MCP (src/mcp): the tools and the embedded App widgets.
  • Web (src/http): login, dashboard, the app views, settings, in the Linear design language.

Quick start

With no DATABASE_URL, Temple boots an in-memory pg-mem database seeded with demo data, so there is zero setup.

npm install
npm test          # engine + RBAC + access + MCP smoke tests
npm run verify    # print the schema verifier report
npm run dev       # web UI + MCP on http://localhost:3000

Set DATABASE_URL to use real PostgreSQL; the schema and demo seed apply on first boot. Demo logins, all with password temple:

EmailRoleCan
marco@incredicorp.devownereverything
ada@incredicorp.devadmineverything
ben@incredicorp.devmemberread / create / update / transition
vera@incredicorp.devviewerread only
agent@incredicorp.devagentread / create / update / transition (no manage)

Connect an agent over MCP

  • HTTP (deployed): add POST https://<host>/mcp as a custom connector in claude.ai.
  • Local stdio: register the server in .mcp.json for Claude Code. Each MCP token is bound to a user and a mode (published or draft).

Entities and the store

Every app's data lives in one entities table. An entity carries an app, a type, a title, an optional state, a JSON properties bag, an optional markdown body, a parent_id for containment, and, since the access layer, an immutable space_id home. Every table is org-scoped, so org_id is the outer hard wall around all data.

This single generic store is why a new app is just a blueprint, not a new schema migration: flow issues, pages pages, and wiki pages are all rows in the same table, distinguished by app and type and validated against their blueprint.

Blueprints

A blueprint is a verified spec, one file in blueprints/ (YAML is the house format; TOML and JSON also parse). It declares entity types, their typed properties, and optionally a state machine. A blueprint is only trusted once the verifier passes it. Ships with three (flow, pages, wiki) plus reference examples (crm, tasks).

Property types available: title, text, richtext, select, multiselect, status, number, date, user, relation, checkbox, url. A relation is a typed foreign key: it names a target entity type and is enforced both statically (the verifier) and at runtime (the bouncer). See Authoring blueprints for the full reference.

The engine (the bouncer)

Every create, update, and transition funnels through one pipeline. The headline tool, request_transition, runs all of it; create and update run the relevant subset. A rejection comes back with a stage and a human-readable reason, so the caller learns why, not just that it failed.

  1. Authenticate to an ActorContext (user, org, role, mode). Already resolved before the call.
  2. Space access (policy stage): can this actor reach this entity at all, by owning its home space or holding a grant?
  3. Policy gate (policy): the RBAC capability, then the per-transition role policy.
  4. From-state legality (validation): is the action legal from the current state?
  5. Property validation + relation FK checks (validation).
  6. Guards (guard): declared preconditions, for example a property must be present.
  7. Effects: pure, computed on the prospective entity (timestamps, revisions, backlinks).
  8. Invariants (invariant): re-checked on the prospective state, must always hold.
  9. Apply + audit + snapshot: one transaction. The row, its audit entry, and its version snapshot land together or not at all.
Rejection stagespolicy, guard, invariant, validation, notfound. The happy path create, start, submit_review, approve produces an audit count of exactly four.

The verifier

A blueprint is run through a four-level gate before it is trusted. Think of it as a Swiss-cheese stack: each level catches a different class of error.

LevelNameCatches
L1algebraduplicate types/properties, a relation pointing at an unknown type, a missing title property, exactly-one-initial-state, unknown from/to states in transitions
L2reachabilitystates unreachable from the initial state, dead-end non-terminal states, terminal states with a non-reopen exit
L3soundnessinvariants that can be violated by a legal transition path (model-check), e.g. entering a state without guaranteeing a required property
L4propertyrandomised legal action sequences asserting invariants always hold (200 runs)

Run npm run verify for the report. A blueprint with any error-severity finding is not published.

Roles and permissions

Five roles, seven permissions. The matrix lives in code (synchronous and testable) and is seeded into role_permissions so the settings UI can show it. Agents are first-class actors with their own role, not a backdoor.

Permissionowneradminmembervieweragent
entity.readyesyesyesyesyes
entity.createyesyesyesnoyes
entity.updateyesyesyesnoyes
entity.transitionyesyesyesnoyes
settings.manageyesyesnonono
roles.manageyesyesnonono
members.manageyesyesnonono

The matrix is the coarse gate. On top of it, individual transitions carry a per-action policy list, so an agent can hold entity.transition in general yet still be blocked from cancel or approve on a flow issue. Both checks run: the permission first, then the transition policy.

Modes: published and draft

Temple runs two parallel worlds. published is production data; draft is an overlay for authoring and trying schema changes safely. An MCP token is minted bound to a user and a mode, so a draft connector cannot touch production data, and a blueprint can be drafted, verified, and published without disturbing the live world. Entities, transitions, and snapshots all carry the mode, so the two never bleed together.

Versioning and time travel

Every governed mutation snapshots the full post-state into entity_snapshots, linked to the transition that produced it, per element and per transaction. Versioned entity types (pages, wiki) additionally write an immutable row to revisions on each edit.

  • list_versions reads the history (version, action, who, state, when).
  • diff_versions compares two versions and renders the property, state, and title changes.
  • revert_entity rolls back. This is not a destructive undo: it re-applies the old state forward as a new audited transition, invariants still enforced, history never rewritten. Reserved for owner and admin.

Spaces and sharing

Access control rests on two orthogonal axes. Confusing them is where most data leaks come from, so Temple keeps them strictly apart.

  • Ownership (the home space): every entity belongs to exactly one space, set at create and immutable. Kinds: personal (one user), team (a named group), company (org-wide). The home space decides where writes land and the foreign-key boundary.
  • Access (grants): who may read, comment, or write a thing, layered on top of ownership. Grants are revocable, audited, and never move data.

Sharing with a person or group is purely the access axis: a personal note shared with a colleague is still in your personal space, they just hold a grant. The only operation that crosses a boundary is the audited transfer_entity (promote). The structural default home for new entities is the shared company space (collaborative); pass space: "personal" or space: "team:<name>" to place something elsewhere.

Safe by asymmetryPersonal-to-shared is the feared direction (a confidentiality breach), so it requires an explicit, confirmed act. Shared-to-personal and revocation are low-friction. The full model, schema, and prompting guide live in the dedicated access-control document.

Flow

A Linear-like issue tracker, and the strict one. A single entity type, issue, with a genuine state machine: backlog (initial), todo, in_progress, in_review, done (terminal), canceled (terminal).

backlog ──plan──▶ todo ──start──▶ in_progress ──submit_review──▶ in_review ──approve──▶ done │ │ ▲ │ └──────start───┘ └────────────reject───────────┘ cancel: any non-terminal ──▶ canceled reopen: done|canceled ──▶ backlog

Transitions carry role policy (cancel and reopen are owner/admin only; approve and reject exclude agents). submit_review guards on assignee being present. approve stamps completed_at. Two invariants always hold: no in_review or done without an assignee, and an estimate, if set, must be zero or greater.

Pages

Notion-like, looser, no hard state machine. Two entity types: database (a container) and page (flexible typed properties plus a markdown body, parented under a database or another page). Pages are versioned: every edit writes a revision. Governance comes from role policy and one invariant, every page keeps a non-empty title.

Wiki

The loosest blueprint: free-form markdown pages in a tree. One entity type, wiki_page: title, optional summary, tags. Two effects fire on every create and update: write_revision appends an immutable revision, and extract_backlinks pulls [[Wiki Link]] targets out of the body so the link graph stays current automatically.

The web UI

The human surface is deliberately thin: login, a dashboard, read views of the three apps, and settings (roles, the permission matrix, members). It reads and writes through the same engine as MCP, so nothing the web app does bypasses the bouncer.

MCP tool reference

Every tool routes through the engine. Plain tools return text or JSON; the show_* tools render widgets. Example outputs are verbatim from the server.

Reading

whoami()
  -> Marco <marco@incredicorp.dev>, role 'owner', mode 'published', org org_demo.

list_blueprints()                          // apps + entity types + verified status
query_entities({ app, type?, state?, q?, limit? })  // raw rows for your own reasoning
get_entity({ id })                          // one entity + the actions legal for you
search({ q, app? })                          // title search across apps

Writing (the bouncer)

create_entity({ app, type, properties, body?, parentId?, space? })
  // space: personal | company | team:<name> | a space id; default company
  -> created ent_a1b2c3 (issue) in state 'backlog'

update_properties({ app, type, id, properties?, body? })
  -> updated ent_a1b2c3      // or: rejected at policy: you do not have write access to ...

request_transition({ app, type, id, action, payload? })
  -> 'start': backlog → in_progress (effects: none)
  -> rejected at guard: guard: 'assignee' must be set

Time travel

list_versions({ id })            // version, action, actor, state, time (newest first)
revert_entity({ app, type, id, version })   // owner/admin; re-applies old state forward
diff_versions({ id, from, to })  // widget: property/state/title changes

Access and sharing

grant_access({ entityId, principal, level, targetKind?, expiresAt? })
  // principal: user email | group name | team name;  level: read|comment|write
  -> shared ent_a1b2c3 with Alice (user) at level 'read'. grant grn_xyz.

revoke_access({ entityId, principal, targetKind? })
list_grants({ entityId })          // who an entity is shared with (read-gated)
transfer_entity({ app, type, id, space })   // the only boundary crossing; audited
  -> transferred ent_a1b2c3: moved spc_personal -> spc_company

Widgets (render UI in the host)

show_board({ app? })   show_record({ id })   show_page({ id })
show_wiki({ id })      show_list({ app?, type?, state?, q?, limit? })   show_access({ id })
When to use whichFor showing the user a collection, prefer show_list over query_entities: it renders a clickable table. Use query_entities only for your own counting and follow-up logic.

Widget gallery

Widgets are MCP App UI rendered inside the host, so a human reviewing an agent's work sees real interfaces, not raw JSON. They follow the Linear-derived design language and respect the host light or dark theme. The board, record, page, and wiki widgets are shown in the app sections above, and the access panel under Spaces and sharing. Below: the adaptive list and the version diff.

Authoring blueprints

A new app is one file. Below is the shape, drawn from the real flow blueprint. Save it in blueprints/, run npm run verify, and it becomes a working, enforced app.

key: flow
name: Flow
kind: flow
version: 1
description: "Linear-like issue tracker."
entities:
  - type: issue
    titleProperty: title
    stateMachine: true
    properties:
      - { name: title, type: title, required: true }
      - { name: assignee, type: user }
      - { name: priority, type: select, options: [none, low, medium, high, urgent], default: none }
      - { name: estimate, type: number }
    states:
      - { name: backlog, initial: true }
      - { name: in_progress }
      - { name: in_review }
      - { name: done, terminal: true }
    transitions:
      - { action: start, from: [backlog], to: in_progress, policy: [owner, admin, member, agent] }
      - action: submit_review
        from: [in_progress]
        to: in_review
        guards: [{ kind: propertyPresent, prop: assignee }]   # precondition
      - action: approve
        from: [in_review]
        to: done
        effects: [{ name: set_timestamp, args: { prop: completed_at } }]
        policy: [owner, admin, member]                          # excludes agent
    invariants:
      - { id: I_review_needs_assignee, kind: requiresPropertyWhenStateIn,
          params: { prop: assignee, states: [in_review, done] } }

Building blocks

  • Property types: title, text, richtext, select, multiselect, status, number, date, user, relation, checkbox, url.
  • Guards: propertyPresent, propertyEquals, hasRelation, declared preconditions on a transition.
  • Invariants: requiresPropertyWhenStateIn, numberMinWhenPresent, requiredPropertyAlways, terminalNoExit, always true on the prospective state.
  • Effects: pure post-computations such as set_timestamp, write_revision, extract_backlinks, fired on named actions.
  • Relations are typed foreign keys; name the target type and the verifier (L1) plus the bouncer enforce integrity.

Loosen the structure by omitting the state machine (like pages) or going fully free-form with versioning and backlinks (like wiki). The same engine runs all of them.

Cookbook

Hands-on recipes. Each shows the calls and the expected result. Phrase them to an agent in natural language; the tool calls are what the agent issues.

R1 Move an issue through its lifecycle

Goal: create an issue and walk it to done, audited at every step.
create_entity({ app:"flow", type:"issue",
  properties:{ title:"Fix login race", assignee:"usr_ada", priority:"high", team:"core" } })
  -> created ent_x (issue) in state 'backlog'
request_transition({ app:"flow", type:"issue", id:"ent_x", action:"start" })
  -> 'start': backlog → in_progress
request_transition({ app:"flow", type:"issue", id:"ent_x", action:"submit_review" })
  -> 'submit_review': in_progress → in_review
request_transition({ app:"flow", type:"issue", id:"ent_x", action:"approve" })
  -> 'approve': in_review → done (effects: set_timestamp)

R2 Learn from a rejection

Goal: see the bouncer teach. A guard and a policy refusal, each with a reason.
// submit_review with no assignee set:
request_transition({ app:"flow", type:"issue", id:"ent_y", action:"submit_review" })
  -> rejected at guard: guard: 'assignee' must be set

// an agent tries to approve (policy excludes agent):
request_transition({ app:"flow", type:"issue", id:"ent_y", action:"approve" })
  -> rejected at policy: action 'approve' is not permitted for role 'agent'

R3 Build a page database and a tree

Goal: a Notion-style database with nested pages.
create_entity({ app:"pages", type:"database",
  properties:{ title:"Product Specs", icon:"▣" } })            -> created ent_db
create_entity({ app:"pages", type:"page", parentId:"ent_db",
  properties:{ title:"Architecture", status:"done", tags:["spec","decision"] },
  body:"# Temple\nOne owned data layer, one MCP bouncer." })    -> created ent_pg

R4 A wiki page with backlinks

Goal: durable text where links maintain themselves.
create_entity({ app:"wiki", type:"wiki_page",
  properties:{ title:"Engineering Handbook", tags:["guide"] },
  body:"Welcome. See [[Deployment Runbook]] and [[Glossary]]." })
  // extract_backlinks fires: the two [[links]] are stored as backlinks automatically

R5 Compare and revert versions

Goal: inspect history and roll back without rewriting it.
list_versions({ id:"ent_pg" })            -> v3 update ... / v2 update ... / v1 create ...
diff_versions({ id:"ent_pg", from:1, to:3 })   // widget: what changed
revert_entity({ app:"pages", type:"page", id:"ent_pg", version:1 })
  -> reverted ent_pg to v1   // a NEW audited version; history intact (owner/admin only)

R6 Draft, verify, publish a schema

Goal: change a blueprint safely in the draft world, then go live.
# 1. author/edit the blueprint file in blueprints/ (draft mode token)
npm run verify          # L1-L4 must pass with zero errors
# 2. publish promotes the verified draft into the published world.
#    Draft entities and published entities never bleed together (separate mode).

R7 Keep something private

Goal: a note only you can see.
create_entity({ app:"pages", type:"page", space:"personal",
  properties:{ title:"My planning notes" }, body:"draft thoughts" })
  // lands in your personal space; other members cannot read or write it

R8 Share with a person or group

Goal: grant access without moving the data.
grant_access({ entityId:"ent_note", principal:"alice@acme.com", level:"read" })
  -> shared ent_note with Alice (user) at level 'read'. grant grn_1.
grant_access({ entityId:"ent_note", principal:"design", level:"write" })   // a group
list_grants({ entityId:"ent_note" })      -> Alice (read), group "design" (write)
revoke_access({ entityId:"ent_note", principal:"alice@acme.com" })         // instant

R9 Promote personal work to the team

Goal: cross the boundary, on purpose, audited.
transfer_entity({ app:"pages", type:"page", id:"ent_note", space:"company" })
  -> transferred ent_note: moved spc_personal -> spc_company
  // now visible org-wide. The only operation that changes an entity's home space.

R10 Ship a brand-new app

Goal: a working, governed app from one file.
# write blueprints/crm.yaml declaring a 'deal' entity with a state machine
npm run verify          # prove it passes L1-L4
# the app is now live: create_entity({ app:"crm", type:"deal", ... }) is enforced end to end

Deploy and operate

  • Local: npm run dev serves the web UI and the MCP endpoint on http://localhost:3000. No DATABASE_URL means in-memory pg-mem with the demo seed.
  • Railway: Nixpacks builds with npm run build and starts node dist/index.js. Add a PostgreSQL plugin, set DATABASE_URL; schema and seed apply on first boot. Healthcheck: /healthz.
  • Env: DATABASE_URL, PORT (3000), SESSION_SECRET, MCP_ALLOWED_ORIGINS (CORS allowlist for the MCP endpoint), NODE_ENV.
  • MCP tokens: portal-minted, bound to a user and a mode (published or draft), hashed at rest, revocable.

Glossary

  • Bouncer: the engine's transition pipeline; the one door every write passes through.
  • Blueprint: a verified spec that defines an app's entity types and rules.
  • Home space: an entity's single immutable owner space (personal, team, company).
  • Grant: revocable access laid on top of ownership; never moves data.
  • Mode: the published or draft world an actor reads and writes.
  • Snapshot: the full post-state of a governed mutation, for time travel.
